what_its_for: Rilonacept is used to treat recurrent pericarditis (repeated episodes of painful inflammation around the heart) and to prevent it from coming back. It works by blocking certain proteins in your body called interleukin-1 (IL-1) that cause inflammation.
how_to_take: Rilonacept is given as a shot (injection) under the skin (subcutaneous injection). Your doctor or nurse will show you how to inject it properly. Common injection sites include the stomach area (abdomen), the front of your thighs, or the upper outer area of your arms. Rotate your injection sites each time — do not inject into the same spot twice in a row. Do not inject into skin that is bruised, red, tender, or hard.
dosing: For adults, the usual starting dose is 320 mg given as two separate 160 mg injections on the same day. After that, you will receive 160 mg once a week. Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to use and when. Always follow your doctor's instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. Then go back to your regular weekly schedule. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Keep rilonacept in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. Do not freeze it — throw it away if it has been frozen. Once removed from the refrigerator, it can be kept at room temperature (up to 77°F / 25°C) for up to 30 days, but must be used before that 30-day period ends. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of used needles and syringes in a proper sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, or nasal flu vaccine) while using rilonacept, as it can make these vaccines less effective or cause infection. Talk to your doctor before any vaccination. Avoid close contact with people who are sick or have an infection, as rilonacept lowers your body's ability to fight infections. Avoid this medication if you have an active infection — tell your doctor right away if you feel sick.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of infection such as fever, chills, sweating, cough, shortness of breath, or burning when you urinate; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing; chest pain or tightness; redness, swelling, or pain at the injection site that does not improve; or if you feel unusually tired or unwell. Tell your doctor if you are scheduled for surgery or any vaccinations.
when_it_works: Many patients begin to notice improvement in their pericarditis symptoms (such as chest pain and inflammation) within the first few weeks of treatment. However, it may take a few months to experience the full benefit. Do not stop taking rilonacept without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better — stopping suddenly can cause your symptoms to return.
special_populations: Children and teenagers: Rilonacept is approved for use in children 12 years of age and older for recurrent pericarditis. The dose is based on body weight for younger patients. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The effects of rilonacept on unborn babies and nursing infants are not fully known. Use effective birth control during treatment. Older adults (65 and over): Older adults may have a higher risk of infections. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions before starting this medication.
